catalog_quote: 1.3 . Tone Mbalanhu appears to be a pitch - accent, rather than a pure tone language such as Nama . From tentative observations four tonemes can be distinguished: high, low, mid - high, and mid - low . The tonology of the dialect ... contrastive tonemes were indicated . High tones were marked throughout the work, while low tones were indicated only where rising or falling tone occur, (e.g. in the case of diphthongs: - láùvé ' black ') ... 1.4 . Orthography ... disjunctive writing style . Firstly, the basis of Doke's (Fivaz, 1986: xviii) conjunctive word division was the phonetic length - stress which occurs (in slow speech) on the penultimate syllable of words in some Bantu languages (e.g. Zulu) . This feature is lacking in the Wambo languages / dialects .

new_statements.rule_in_words: Fourie treats Mbalanhu as a pitch accent (not 'pure tone') language with lexically marked high tones (two contrastive tonemes marked, four tentatively heard) and states explicitly that the penultimate length-stress typical of Zulu-type Bantu languages does not exist in the Wambo languages/dialects, Mbalanhu included. No position for a word accent or stress is given anywhere in the sketch; prominence is carried by lexical/grammatical tone.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Tone: rising/falling contours arise on diphthongs (p.30); 'long tone' on identical vowel sequences (p.6). Author flags the tonology as tentative and under-studied.
new_statements.domain_note: The negative stress statement is made for the whole Wambo (R.20) cluster in the context of orthographic word division (citing Fivaz 1986: xviii for Ndonga); the pitch accent characterisation is specific to the Mbalanhu dialect. Tone marks based on Visi-Pitch profiles of one main speaker (Ms Sara Andjaba), verified with others (p.3).
new_statements.identity_note: Fourie 1993 describes the Mbalanhu dialect (Glottolog mbal1262; Omusati region, Namibia; c. 50,320 speakers per the sketch), one of three dialects Glottolog groups under Central Wambo mbal1255 (the others, Mbadja mbad1234 and Dombondola domd1234, are Angolan and undescribed). The explicit no-penultimate-stress statement is made for 'the Wambo languages/dialects' as a whole (R.20 cluster incl. Ndonga ndon1254 and Kwanyama kuan1247); the 'pitch accent rather than pure tone language' characterisation is Mbalanhu-specific.

tone_statements.citation: Halme(-Berneking), Riikka. 2014. Melodic High in Mbadja and Kwanyama. Africana Linguistica 20(1): 145-161. doi:10.3406/aflin.2014.1028
tone_statements.quote: Mbadja is a two‑tone system with High and Low tones, reflecting the reconstructed Proto‑Bantu tones. Non‑initial stem vowels are analyzed as underlyingly toneless, and they are assigned a Low tone by default. The High and Low tones are realized with a relatively high and low level pitch, respectively. In a sequence of High tones, the last High tone before a Low tone is usually higher than the preceding High tones. Automatic downstepping occurs so that a High tone following a Low tone is realized with a slightly lower pitch than the preceding High tone.
tone_statements.locator: p. 146 (introduction, 'basics of Mbadja tone'); abstract on the record page gives the four melodic-High patterns
tone_statements.summary: Mbadja (Central Wambo dialect): 2 level tones H vs L (privative H, toneless vowels default L), automatic downstep, H raising before L; verb TAM paradigms select among 4 melodic High patterns; a full lexical/grammatical tone system rather than Fourie's tentative 'pitch accent' label for Mbalanhu.

sources.locator: p. 146 (introduction, 'basics of Mbadja tone'); abstract on the record page gives the four melodic-High patterns
sources.note: Full text (p.146) states Mbadja is a two-tone (H/L) system reflecting Proto-Bantu tones, non-initial stem vowels underlyingly toneless (default L), raised last H before L, automatic downstep; the paper identifies four melodic High patterns in the verb system (no stem melodic H; melodic H from V2 to final; V2 to penult in one form; H on final vowel in one form), distinct behaviour of H verb stems in Polarized/O-forms and main-clause negatives, and compares Mbadja with Kwanyama (minor differences).

sources.note: The only full prosodic analysis of any variety in the Wambo (R.20) dialect cluster (Kwanyama, kuan1247, 85% mutually intelligible with Mbalanhu per Baucom 1972:47).
